    1                                                   I. INTRODUCTION

    2    Q.     Please state your name, business address, and position.

    3    A.     My name is Adrian J. Kimbrough, and my business address is 417 Denison Street,

    4           Highland Park, New Jersey 08904. I am employed as a Senior Vice President at Gabel

    5           Associates, Inc., an energy, environmental, and public utility consulting firm.

    6    Q.     Are you the same Adrian J. Kimbrough who filed responsive and rebuttal testimony

    7           in this proceeding?

    8    A.     Yes.

    9    Q.     What is the purpose and organization of your surrebuttal testimony?

   10    A.     My surrebuttal testimony responds to the October 5, 2026, rebuttal testimony of Oklahoma

   11           Gas and Electric Company (“OG&E”) witnesses Matthew DeCourcey, Gwin Cash, John

   12           P. Laws, Kimber L. Shoop, Kelly Riley, and Adam Snapp, as well as the rebuttal testimony

   13           of Petroleum Alliance of Oklahoma (“PAO”) witness Dr. David E. Dismukes. Following

   14           this Introduction, my testimony is organized into eight substantive sections matching the

   15           core disputed issues in this docket: (II) Customer-Funded Self-Supply (“Rider SSS”), (III)

   16           the Pre-Service Reservation Charge, (IV) the Customer Class Protection Charge, (V) the

   17           Customer Affordability Charge, (VI) Billing Minimums, (VII) Early Termination and

   18           Capacity Reduction, (VIII) Contract Term, Renewal, and Load Ramp, and (IX) Financial

   19           Security and Collateral, followed by a Conclusion (Section X) and an updated Testimony

   20           Summary.

    1    Q.        Please summarize your surrebuttal conclusions and whether the rebuttal testimony

    2              changes your recommendations.

    3    A.        None of the rebuttal testimony changes the core policy and tariff-design recommendations

    4              set forth in my responsive and rebuttal testimony.1 I agree with OG&E and the other parties

    5              in this proceeding that Schedule XLPL must establish strong, enforceable protections so

    6              that existing Oklahoma ratepayers do not bear the infrastructure costs or risks of serving

    7              new large loads. Where my recommendations differ from OG&E’s proposal, the goal is to

    8              ensure that each tariff charge and contract obligation is aligned with documented cost

    9              causation, actual utility exposure, and established ratemaking principles so that the tariff is

   10              both protective of existing customers and commercially workable for large-load

   11              investment.

   12                       First, on generation supply, I recommend that the Commission approve Rider SSS

   13              as a voluntary option for full and partial customer-funded self-supply. Allowing Extra

   14              Large Power and Light (“XLPL”) customers to bring their own Southwest Power Pool

   15              (“SPP”)-accredited capacity equal to 100 percent of their self-supplied peak demand plus

   16              the full prevailing SPP Planning Reserve Margin (“PRM”) insulates existing residential

   17              and small-business customers from higher-cost marginal generation additions, addresses

   18              OG&E’s concern regarding imputed debt on third-party capacity contracts, and preserves

   19              100 percent recovery of OG&E’s transmission delivery and administrative costs.

   20                       Second, I recommend that the Commission decline to adopt OG&E’s three

   21              proposed surcharges that are not tied to specific service costs—the Pre-Service Reservation

   16               Rider SSS—which OG&E refers to as “DODGE” (“Delivery Only Deregulated Generation

   19                   while the risks of supplier default, accreditation changes, or PPA expiration are

   20                   significant, arguing that OG&E could be required to act as the physical backstop and

   21                   shift unrecovered costs onto existing customers.3

    1    Q.      How do you respond to these rebuttal arguments regarding Rider SSS?

    2    A.      While OG&E’s witnesses raise operational and resource-adequacy concerns, each of those

    3            concerns is directly addressed by the tariff safeguards in Rider SSS and the record in this

    4            proceeding.

    5            ● First, Rider SSS does not require OG&E to provide uncompensated standby or

    6                backstop generation service, because a participating customer must satisfy the same

    7                SPP accreditation and reserve-margin standards that apply to OG&E. Under Rider SSS,

    8                a customer must supply SPP-accredited, deliverable capacity equal to 100 percent of

    9                its self-supplied peak demand plus the full prevailing SPP Planning Reserve Margin,

   10                and all hourly energy imbalances settle directly at the SPP Locational Marginal Price

   11                (“LMP”).9

   12                    Because a full self-supply customer satisfies 100 percent of its load and reserve-

   13                margin obligation, OG&E does not need to plan or hold standby or backup generation

   14                for that self-supplied load. Where a customer elects partial self-supply, the customer

   15                contracts upfront in its ESA for a defined tranche of bundled Supplemental Utility

   16                Capacity from OG&E and pays OG&E’s full bundled generation rates and minimums

   17                on that utility-supplied tranche.10

   18                    Furthermore, to address Witness Riley’s question regarding potential declines in

   19                seasonal SPP Effective Load Carrying Capability (“ELCC”) accreditation or PPA

   20                expiration,11 I recommend clarifying Section 3.04 of Rider SSS to establish that it is

    1               citing a recently filed Indiana Michigan Power rate case. Is downward pressure on

    4               customers’ rates depends largely on three utility-specific factors: (1) the level of the

    5               utility’s existing embedded rates, (2) whether the utility has available accredited capacity

    6               headroom, and (3) the marginal cost of new generation relative to embedded cost:

    7               ● First, where a utility has relatively high embedded generation demand rates (such as

    9                   DeCourcey),24 possesses existing system capacity headroom, or faces moderate

   10                   incremental supply costs, adding a high-load-factor (85 to 90+ percent) customer

   11                   spreads fixed costs over a larger billing base and could place downward pressure on

   12                   average rates. That same beneficial downward pressure occurs on shared transmission

   13                   and delivery costs when a customer funds dedicated interconnection facilities upfront

   14                   through CIAC and self-supplies its generation under Rider SSS.

   15               ● Second, where a utility has lower embedded rates (such as OG&E’s $7.08/kW-month

   16                   SL-1 demand charge, which covers both transmission and generation), no excess

   17                   headroom, and higher marginal costs, rolling new utility generation into pooled

   18                   embedded rates can place upward pressure on average rates. For example, OG&E’s
